strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time scaling and controllable generation for diffusion models using verifier-guided search.
The proposed framing that combines local Langevin-style refinement with global tree-search variants is conceptually clean and applies across differentiable and non-differentiable verifiers.
The empirical scope is broader than much related work, covering long-horizon maze planning, offline RL, compositional text-to-image generation, and ImageNet conditional generation.
Results generally support the claim that verifier-guided search can improve compute efficiency over naive best-of-N sampling, especially in maze planning and the BFS/DFS image experiments.
The paper is mostly well organized, with pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameter tables, and appendices that make the methods reasonably understandable.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: BFS/resampling/pruning and DFS/backtracking closely resemble known particle filtering, SMC, beam search, rejection/backtracking, and recent diffusion inference-time scaling methods; the paper would benefit from sharper positioning and direct comparisons to these alternatives.

The theoretical contribution is limited and partly informal. The claimed equivalence between recurrent training-free guidance and Langevin MCMC is asymptotic, relies on hand-waved existence of annealed verifier functions and continuous-limit arguments, and does not provide finite-step guarantees or clarify when the practical algorithm samples from the intended composed distribution.

Several empirical settings rely on privileged or oracle verifiers, such as exact maze geometry, pretrained Q-functions, BLIP/UniDet task oracles, and classifiers; this makes the practical significance less clear when verifiers are noisy, biased, or misaligned.

The evaluation is not uniformly convincing. Offline RL is competitive but not better than the strongest baselines on average, uses inherited pretrained models/Q-functions, and mostly uses very small particle counts, so it provides limited evidence for the proposed global search methods.
The ImageNet conditional generation experiment is narrow, using only two class labels and relatively poor absolute FID/accuracy, which weakens claims about general conditional generation.

Ablations are incomplete: there is limited isolation of local versus global components across all domains, limited sensitivity analysis for thresholds/temperatures/backtracking depth, and limited study of verifier hacking despite acknowledging it as a core risk.

Compute accounting and hyperparameter tuning are not fully satisfactory. The method appears to require substantial tuning and over 1000 GPU hours, but the paper does not consistently separate tuning compute from inference compute or show robustness to hyperparameter choices.

Reproducibility is only moderate: many details are provided, but the project link appears blank in the manuscript text, and there is no clear indication that code, trained models, or exact evaluation scripts are available.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: improving diffusion-model outputs at inference time using verifier-guided search, with potential relevance to planning, RL, and image generation.

The proposed framing of local verifier-gradient refinement and global denoising-tree exploration is intuitive and could be useful as a unifying perspective for several existing guidance and search methods.
The experiments span multiple domains rather than a single benchmark, and the paper includes useful implementation details and pseudocode in the appendix.
The empirical results suggest that intermediate verifier-based resampling/pruning can be more compute-efficient than naive best-of-N sampling in some settings.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Much of the method appears to be a repackaging of existing training-free guidance, recurrence/Langevin refinement, particle resampling, pruning, and best-of-N search under classical-search terminology. The actual algorithmic contributions are relatively straightforward.

The central theoretical claim is weakly supported. Proposition 1 is an informal continuous-limit equivalence between recurrence-based guidance and Langevin MCMC, but the paper does not provide finite-step guarantees, convergence analysis under practical schedules, or a convincing treatment of approximation errors introduced by learned scores and surrogate verifiers.

The evaluation is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. ImageNet conditional generation is tested on only two class labels with very poor absolute FID/accuracy, making it hard to assess generality. CompBench comparisons are mainly against best-of-N rather than strong recent inference-time diffusion-scaling baselines. The planning experiments rely on ground-truth maze-layout verifiers and a custom harder maze, which limits external validity.

The offline RL results are not compelling as a main contribution: the method is roughly tied with or slightly below prior QGPO/Diffusion-QL averages, uses pretrained diffusion policies and Q-functions from prior work, and demonstrates only modest gains relative to strong baselines.

Compute efficiency is asserted but not rigorously normalized. The paper uses many hyperparameter searches, verifier calls, recurrence steps, particles, and more than 1000 GPU hours, but the reported comparisons do not consistently account for tuning cost, verifier cost, wall-clock time, or equal-quality/equal-budget tradeoffs.

Verifier hacking and robustness are under-addressed. The paper acknowledges adversarial samples and introduces a double-verifier heuristic, but this is evaluated narrowly and does not resolve the broader concern that optimizing against imperfect verifiers may produce misleading improvements.

Reproducibility and presentation are weaker than expected: the project page field is blank, several experimental choices are buried in the appendix, some plots are hard to interpret from the text alone, and important baselines/ablations are missing or incomplete.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely formulation of inference-time scaling for diffusion models as search over the denoising process, combining gradient-based local refinement with BFS/DFS-style global exploration.

The local-search contribution is conceptually useful: connecting training-free guidance with recurrence to annealed Langevin MCMC provides a principled lens that unifies several prior guidance methods and helps explain why recurrence can reduce off-manifold/adversarial behavior.
The empirical scope is broader than typical diffusion guidance papers, covering long-horizon maze planning, offline RL, compositional text-to-image generation, and ImageNet conditional generation.

The experiments generally support the main practical claim that verifier-guided inference-time search can improve compute efficiency over naive best-of-N sampling, especially in maze planning and image-generation settings.
The paper is well organized and includes useful implementation details, pseudocode, hyperparameter descriptions, and discussion of verifier hacking and hyperparameter-tuning limitations.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly incremental: BFS/DFS, best-of-N, resampling, pruning, restart/backtracking, SMC-like steering, and training-free guidance are all closely related to prior work. The paper's main contribution is a unifying framework plus empirical synthesis rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic primitive.

The theoretical result is mostly asymptotic and informal in its implications for the practical algorithms. Proposition 1 depends on continuous-limit reasoning and does not provide finite-step error bounds or conditions under which the implemented guidance/search procedures approximate the target composed distribution well.

Several empirical claims rely on relatively limited or narrow evaluations. The ImageNet conditional generation experiment uses only two labels, and the offline RL results are competitive but not clearly better than strong training-based baselines on average.

The evaluation would be stronger with more systematic ablations isolating local search, global search, verifier choice, double-verifier design, threshold/temperature schedules, and hyperparameter tuning cost across all domains.

The method depends heavily on verifier quality and access. In some settings the verifier is an oracle or ground-truth simulator-like signal, which makes the practical generality less clear. The risk of verifier hacking is acknowledged but not deeply evaluated.

Compute efficiency is central to the paper, but the accounting is not always fully normalized across verifier calls, gradient computations, backtracking, local-search recurrence steps, and hyperparameter search overhead.

Reproducibility is moderate rather than excellent: many details are given, but the paper does not make clear whether code, trained models, exact prompts/seeds, and full per-task hyperparameter sweeps will be released.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and coherent framing of inference-time scaling for diffusion models through classical search, unifying global search over denoising trajectories with local gradient-based refinement.

The BFS design-space analysis is useful: it clarifies how several recent particle/tree-search methods relate and identifies practical choices such as SSP resampling, max scoring, and increasing tempering.
The DFS-style backtracking idea is simple, intuitive, and potentially valuable for adaptive compute allocation; the CompBench experiments suggest it can improve the quality-compute tradeoff.

The paper evaluates across multiple domains, including text-to-image generation, long-horizon planning, offline RL, and conditional ImageNet generation, which supports the generality of the framework.

The local-search discussion gives a helpful connection between recurrent training-free guidance and Langevin MCMC, and the experiments show that combining local and global search can outperform scaling either alone.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat overstated. Much of the framework appears to repackage existing SMC/tree-search/guidance methods, and the new algorithmic ingredients are mainly heuristic combinations and schedules rather than a clearly distinct method with strong theoretical guarantees.

The theoretical claims are limited by restrictive assumptions. The convergence theorem assumes strong log-concavity, smoothness, bounded support, and Lipschitz Hessian conditions that are far from realistic for diffusion model distributions, so it does not substantively justify the practical settings studied.

The evaluation relies heavily on verifier-based objectives, which creates a risk of optimizing the metric rather than true sample quality. This is especially concerning for image tasks, where VLM/classifier scores and small-sample FID are imperfect proxies; human evaluation or stronger independent metrics are missing.

Several empirical gains are modest or within overlapping error bars, particularly in the BFS comparisons, yet the paper makes strong claims about new Pareto frontiers and superiority over prior methods.

Compute accounting is not fully convincing. Counting NFEs may understate the cost of verifier gradients, recurrence, backtracking, and classifier/VLM evaluation, making efficiency comparisons potentially unfair across methods.

The offline RL evaluation is difficult to interpret because it composes pretrained diffusion policies with learned Q-functions and compares partly against training-based baselines; the setup does not cleanly isolate whether the search method itself is responsible for the gains.
The DFS method depends on threshold schedules, backtracking depth, evaluation steps, and verifier calibration, but sensitivity and failure modes are not sufficiently explored.

The double-verifier reward-hacking experiment is interesting but preliminary: it uses only 256 generated samples for FID, related classifier-family verifiers, and limited evidence that the approach prevents more general over-optimization.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the project link appears blank in the manuscript text, implementation details are spread across appendices, and some plots lack precise numeric results.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and timely problem: inference-time control and scaling for diffusion models using verifier-guided search.
It offers a unifying view of several particle/tree-search methods and includes useful ablations over BFS design choices such as resampling, scoring, and tempering.
The empirical scope is broad, covering text-to-image generation, planning, offline RL, and reward-hacking mitigation, which makes the proposed framework potentially relevant across subareas.
The DFS/backtracking idea is simple and practically appealing, and the paper provides evidence that adaptive compute allocation can improve efficiency on some verifier-scored tasks.
weaknesses: The novelty is substantially overstated. Much of the method appears to repackage existing SMC/tree-search, recurrence, restart, and training-free guidance ideas under classical-search terminology; the new algorithmic content beyond combinations and scheduling choices is limited.

The theoretical claims are weak relative to the paper's language. The Langevin/recurrence equivalence is asymptotic and relies on assumptions such as strong log-concavity, smoothness, bounded support, and infinitesimal step sizes that are unrealistic for modern diffusion models and verifier objectives. This does not convincingly justify claims of asymptotically exact or principled sampling in the actual implemented setting.

The evaluation relies heavily on verifier-aligned metrics, which risks measuring optimization of the scoring function rather than true sample quality or task success. This is especially concerning because the paper itself demonstrates reward hacking, but the main image-generation results still depend on learned verifiers without sufficiently strong independent evaluation such as human studies or robust perceptual metrics.

Several experiments are too small or underpowered for the claims. For example, the ImageNet conditional-generation reward-hacking experiment uses only 256 samples, and some RL/planning results report limited seeds or small sample counts with high variance.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. Some baselines are reimplemented or configured differently, compute accounting is not always transparent, and the paper sometimes compares against methods that require training while emphasizing test-time-only advantages, making the practical tradeoffs hard to assess.

Offline RL gains are modest and inconsistent: the proposed method is approximately tied with or slightly below strong baselines on average, while several per-task results have large variance. This does not support the strong claim of establishing a new Pareto frontier across decision-making domains.

The planning setup uses a custom maze and a verifier based on known maze geometry, which may not reflect realistic learned or imperfect verifiers. Generalization beyond this constructed setting is unclear.

Reproducibility is limited. The project link in the abstract appears blank, code is not provided in the manuscript, and many results depend on substantial hyperparameter sweeps and over 1000 GPU hours, making independent verification difficult.

The paper's breadth comes at the cost of depth. Each domain receives relatively limited analysis, and the central claims about joint local/global scaling would benefit from more controlled ablations, stronger baselines, and clearer failure-mode analysis.

The writing makes many strong claims, including 'first' and 'new Pareto frontier,' that are not adequately supported given concurrent work, closely related prior methods, and the limited empirical margins.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: inference-time scaling and controllable diffusion generation are important, and the paper frames global search, local search, and verifier-guided sampling in a coherent way.

The unified BFS design space is useful: the paper clearly relates several recent particle/tree-search methods as special cases and provides practical ablations over resampling, scoring, and tempering choices.
The DFS-style adaptive backtracking idea is simple, appealing, and empirically promising, especially for allocating more compute to harder instances without knowing prompt difficulty in advance.

The paper evaluates across multiple domains, including text-to-image generation, long-horizon planning, offline RL, and conditional ImageNet generation, which supports the claim that the framework is broadly applicable.

The local-search connection to annealed Langevin MCMC provides a principled interpretation of recurrent training-free guidance, and the empirical results suggest that combining local and global search can improve compute-quality tradeoffs.
The double-verifier experiment identifies a real failure mode, verifier over-optimization, and proposes a lightweight mitigation that improves several reported metrics.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental in parts: BFS is largely a synthesis and tuning of existing SMC/tree-search methods, while DFS/backtracking resembles recent restart/cyclic/search-based diffusion inference methods. The paper positions this well, but the conceptual advance may be less large than the framing suggests.

Several key empirical claims rely on verifier scores or task-specific proxy metrics rather than stronger downstream evaluation. For text-to-image, the main evidence appears to be VLM/ImageReward-style scoring rather than human preference, robust compositional metrics, or broader qualitative analysis.

Some evaluations are small or fragile: the ImageNet double-verifier FID is computed on only 256 samples, which is too few for stable FID conclusions, and offline RL uses relatively small seed/sample counts with mixed gains over strong baselines.

The theory is useful for interpretation but does not fully justify the practical finite-step algorithm. The continuous-limit equivalence and convergence discussion depend on assumptions that may not hold for neural diffusion models, biased denoised estimates, or non-smooth learned verifiers.

Hyperparameter dependence remains substantial. Thresholds, backtracking depth, evaluation timesteps, temperatures, particle counts, recurrence/local-search steps, and guidance strengths are all tuned per domain, which weakens claims of a general plug-and-play framework.

The planning experiments use a verifier derived from privileged maze geometry, and the paper acknowledges that the verifier alone does not guarantee success. This makes it harder to assess how well the method would transfer to learned or noisy verifiers.

The offline RL section compares against training-based methods but also uses pretrained Q-functions and carefully tuned inference-time search; the fairness and practical compute tradeoffs would be clearer with wall-clock costs, tuning budgets, and stronger comparisons under equal total resources.

Some claims are overstated, especially around establishing a new Pareto frontier and being the first to jointly scale local and global search. The paper would benefit from more cautious positioning relative to concurrent adaptive/cyclic/evolutionary diffusion search work.
